newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to lose out in ECB profit transfers - paper.
newsitem.headline: Germany to lose out in ECB profit transfers - paper.

text.p: The transfer of monetary policy control to the European Central Bank from 1999 will bring a loss of income for Bonn's budget coffers, the Handelsblatt newspaper reported on Monday, quoting the German finance ministry.

Under the terms of quotas set up for distributing profits from the European Central Bank, Bonn will receive a smaller amount of central bank profit than would be the case if the Bundesbank continued to exist in its current form, it said.
Forecasts by independent economists have already predicted a theoretical loss of income to the government due to the handover of monetary policy control to the European body.

The newspaper quoted comments written by Hansgeorg Hauser, state secretary to the finance ministry, and addressed to Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, the financial expert for the opposition Social Democrat Party, confirming the lower transfer expectations.

"If the current balance sheet structures of the European Union central banks were to remain, then it would be true that the German Bundesbank would be a net payer in the distribution of income within the European System of Central Banks," the newspaper quoted Hauser as writing.
Hauser referred to a statement to this effect from the Bundesbank, the newspaper said.
Comment was not immediately available from the finance ministry.
A Bundesbank spokesman confirmed that the central bank had prepared a statement for the finance ministry in response to its enquiries but declined to comment on its contents.
Under the terms of the European Central Bank regulations, Germany stands to take about 25 percent of the ECB's profit once the central bank has taken over the monetary policy reins.
But high usage of marks in other countries apart from Germany means that the German central bank currently controls a larger proportion of the total profits of the expected future central bank.
The newspaper quoted financial experts as assessing the likely loss to Bonn at four billion marks ($2.1 billion) annually. For 1996, the central bank transferred 8.8 billion in profit to Bonn.

Hauser said in the letter that it was hard to assess the level of profit losses. The Bundesbank was planning to call for a special regulation to be implemented which would boost Bonn's share of ECB profits in the first five years, he added.
A decision on this would be made by the ECB itself.
